title: The Busy Seventh Month Festivals
overview: This chapter lists the offerings for the festivals of the seventh month, Israel's most crowded season of worship: a day of trumpets, a solemn day of atonement, and a week-long harvest festival with a closing day.

parts.label: Day of trumpets (vv. 1-6)
parts.note: The seventh month fell in early autumn, the quiet gap between harvest and planting, and its first day was marked by trumpet blasts and rest from work. Its offerings were added on top of the usual daily and new moon offerings, not swapped for them; later Jewish tradition made this day the New Year, Rosh Hashanah.

parts.label: Day of Atonement (vv. 7-11)
parts.note: On the tenth day the people were to humble themselves through self-denial, traditionally understood as fasting, on the day set aside for clearing the nation's wrongs before God, described in Leviticus 16. This passage adds more offerings to that day's main rituals, including an extra goat to cover wrongdoing.

parts.label: Festival of Shelters begins (vv. 12-16)
parts.note: Five days later came a joyful seven-day harvest festival, when people lived in temporary shelters to remember Israel's years in the desert. It called for more animals than any other festival, starting with thirteen bulls on the first day.

parts.label: The shrinking count (vv. 17-34)
parts.note: Each day the number of bulls drops by one, from thirteen down to seven, adding up to seventy over the week. The text gives no reason; some suggest it eased the cost over time, and an old Jewish tradition linked the seventy bulls to the seventy nations of the world, but no one knows for sure.

parts.label: The closing day (vv. 35-38)
parts.note: An eighth day ended the festival with a solemn gathering and a much smaller offering of just one bull. Christians recall that Jesus spoke on the last great day of this festival in John 7, though scholars are unsure whether that means the seventh day or this eighth one.

parts.label: On top of personal gifts (vv. 39-40)
parts.note: All these were public offerings made on behalf of the whole nation. Personal promises and voluntary gifts to God were still expected in addition, and Moses passed every instruction on to the people.

think: What might it do to a community to set aside, in the same season, both a day of sorrow over its wrongs and a long week of shared celebration?
